masterNotes.context: Achebe published *Things Fall Apart* in 1958 while working for the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation, writing in English but shaping the prose around Igbo speech rhythms and proverb. It became the founding text of modern African literature in English, launching Heinemann's African Writers Series and answering, deliberately, the flattened depictions of Africa in earlier European fiction Achebe later criticized directly in his own essays. The novel opens in the Igbo village of Umuofia before the arrival of European missionaries and administrators, introducing Okonkwo, a man whose standing rests on physical strength and discipline, and whose fear of resembling his gentle, indebted father, Unoka, shapes nearly everything he does. These notes follow the opening chapter.
masterNotes.form: Achebe narrates in close but not fully interior third person, adopting the pacing and communal authority of oral storytelling within English prose, proverbs are woven into the narration itself, not only into dialogue, as a shared measure of wisdom. The opening chapter moves fluidly between Okonkwo's present standing in the village and an extended flashback into his father Unoka's life and death, delaying any forward action to first establish the values by which this community judges a man. Even Unoka's death is rendered in the same measured, unsensational register as everything else, a restraint that lets custom itself carry the emotional weight.
keyImages: Okonkwo's fame from a wrestling match against Amalinze the Cat, still remembered by the village years afterward.
Unoka's flute-playing and mounting debts, presented as the opposite of everything Okonkwo has built his reputation on.
The account of Unoka's death from a swelling illness considered an abomination to the earth goddess, left to die in the Evil Forest without burial.
Okonkwo's visible impatience with anyone in his household who reminds him, even faintly, of his father.
whatToNotice: Notice that Okonkwo is introduced entirely through reputation and comparison before the narration gives any direct physical description.
Notice how long the chapter lingers on Unoka before returning to Okonkwo's present life, and what that delay suggests about what shaped him.
Notice the proverbs offered as communal wisdom within the narration itself, not just as something a character says aloud.
Notice the specific, unsentimental detail given to the customs surrounding Unoka's death and burial.
Notice that the narrator names fear plainly as Okonkwo's central motivation, rather than leaving it for the reader to infer.
discussionQuestions: How does opening with Okonkwo's reputation, rather than his private thoughts, shape your first understanding of him?
What does the extended account of Unoka's failures suggest about how Umuofia measures a man's worth?
How do the proverbs woven into the narration change the novel's voice compared to a more conventional English narrative style?

Beyond the opening chapter: Okonkwo's fear of resembling his father recurs in his dealings with his own children later in the novel — what in the opening chapter already signals how costly that fear might become?
furtherReading: Chinua Achebe's essay "An Image of Africa" — his direct critique of Joseph Conrad's *Heart of Darkness*, useful context for what this novel was written to answer.
Achebe's *No Longer at Ease* — a loosely connected later novel following a descendant of this world into a colonial-era city.
Ezenwa-Ohaeto's *Chinua Achebe: A Biography* — a standard critical biography of the author.

title: The Tyger
author: William Blake

source.name: William Blake, Songs of Innocence and of Experience (1794)

text:
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies,
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp?

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

externalLinks.label: Search Poetry Foundation for this poem

masterNotes.context: Blake wrote "The Tyger" for Songs of Experience (1794), the companion volume to his earlier Songs of Innocence (1789); the two were eventually issued together as Songs of Innocence and of Experience, Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul. Blake was a printmaker as well as a poet, and he etched, hand-colored, and self-published both books rather than working through a conventional printer — the poem's original page carries his own illustration of the tiger. "The Tyger" answers, almost as a direct rebuttal, "The Lamb" from the earlier volume, in which a child asks a lamb who made it and answers confidently: God, who is also a lamb. Here the same question is asked of something fearsome, and the poem never supplies Blake's earlier easy answer. It has become one of the most anthologized poems in English, largely because it refuses to resolve its own central question.
masterNotes.form: Every stanza but the last is built entirely from questions, and Blake never answers a single one directly — the poem interrogates the tiger's maker rather than describing the tiger itself. The insistent trochaic rhythm ("TY-ger TY-ger") gives the poem a hammering, forge-like beat that matches its central conceit of the creator as blacksmith, working with hammer, chain, furnace, and anvil. The rhymed couplets tighten the pressure stanza by stanza, and the final stanza almost exactly repeats the first — except "Could frame" becomes "Dare frame," a single-word change that quietly shifts the whole poem from wonder toward something closer to accusation.
keyImages: "The forests of the night" — the tiger appears already inside a landscape charged with mystery and menace rather than lit by daylight.
The forge imagery of "the hammer," "the chain," "the anvil," and "the furnace" — the creator recast as a blacksmith laboring over something dangerous rather than a gentle craftsman.
"When the stars threw down their spears / And water'd heaven with their tears" — a cosmic image of surrender or grief whose exact meaning the poem never explains.
The final line's single altered word, "Dare frame" replacing "Could frame" — the same question returning with its emotional register changed.
whatToNotice: Notice that almost every line in the poem is a question, and count how many actually get answered.
Notice the forge vocabulary arriving in the third and fourth stanzas — hammer, chain, furnace, anvil — and what kind of maker that implies.
In the fifth stanza, notice the poem widens suddenly from the tiger's body to "the stars" and "heaven," without explanation.
Compare the first and last stanzas line by line; notice exactly which word changes.
Notice the poem never once describes the tiger's stripes, size, or behavior — only the terror and awe of imagining who could have made it.
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that Blake asks whether the same god made both "the Lamb" and the tiger, without answering?
Why might Blake choose a hammering, sing-song rhythm for a poem about something as frightening as a tiger?
Does the shift from "Could frame" to "Dare frame" change your sense of who is doing the daring — the maker, or the reader questioning the maker?
What is gained by describing the tiger entirely through the reaction it provokes, rather than through direct physical description?
furtherReading: "The Lamb" (Blake, *Songs of Innocence*) — the poem "The Tyger" is answering, asking the same question of a gentler creature.
*Songs of Innocence and of Experience* (full volume) — for the "two contrary states" frame Blake built the poem within.
Northrop Frye, *Fearful Symmetry: A Study of William Blake* — a foundational critical study that takes its title directly from this poem.

masterNotes.context: Borges published this story in Spanish in 1941, later collected in *Ficciones* (1944); Donald A. Yates's English translation, used here, appeared in the 1962 anthology *Labyrinths*, the volume that introduced Borges to a wide English-language readership and shaped a generation of writers working in fabulist and postmodern modes. The story presents itself as a document from the First World War: a British historian's account of a delayed German artillery offensive, followed by a found statement from a Chinese scholar turned German spy, Yu Tsun, explaining what happened. These notes follow the story's opening frame, before any of the spy plot itself unfolds.
masterNotes.form: Borges opens the story as a nested document rather than as ordinary narration: an editorial historical note, citing a real-seeming work of military history, gives way to Yu Tsun's own first-person statement, itself introduced as incomplete. This framing device blurs documentary authority and invented testimony from the very first sentence, a technique Borges returns to across his fiction, and it primes the reader to distrust exactly the kind of fact-citing precision the story keeps offering.
keyImages: The opening citation attributing to a historian's account of the war a detail about a delayed artillery offensive, presented with scholarly precision before any story proper begins.
The editorial note's claim that the first pages of Yu Tsun's statement are missing, so the reader enters an already incomplete account.
Yu Tsun identifying himself and his urgent circumstance in the opening lines of his own statement, contrasting sharply with the cool historical framing that precedes it.
The abrupt shift in register between the historian's detached citation and Yu Tsun's immediate, personal voice.
whatToNotice: Notice that the story opens not with action but with a citation to a work of history, immediately blurring documented fact and invention.
Notice that the editorial note announces missing pages before Yu Tsun's account even starts, priming distrust of everything that follows.
Notice how quickly Yu Tsun states his own name and situation once his statement begins, compared to the impersonal historian's note before it.
Notice the contrast in tone between the clinical framing device and the urgent personal voice it introduces.
Notice how much authority the story borrows from the mere form of a citation and a footnote, before offering any evidence.
discussionQuestions: What effect does opening with a citation to a real-seeming historical work have on how you read everything that follows?
Why might Borges have the editorial note announce missing pages before Yu Tsun's statement even begins?
How does framing personal testimony inside a scholarly-sounding footnote change the authority a reader grants it?
Beyond the opening frame: given that pages of Yu Tsun's statement are already missing, how much should a reader trust the account as it continues?
furtherReading: Borges's *Other Inquisitions* — nonfiction essays revisiting his recurring fascination with labyrinths and infinite branching structures.
Borges's story "The Library of Babel" — another metaphysical fiction built on an infinite, ordered structure.
Emir Rodríguez Monegal's *Jorge Luis Borges: A Literary Biography* — a standard critical biography.

title: The Bet
author: Anton Chekhov
excerpt:
The Bet

I

It was a dark autumn night. The old banker was walking up and down his study and remembering how, fifteen years before, he had given a party one autumn evening. There had been many clever men there, and there had been interesting conversations. Among other things they had talked of capital punishment. The majority of the guests, among whom were many journalists and intellectual men, disapproved of the death penalty. They considered that form of punishment out of date, immoral, and unsuitable for Christian states. In the opinion of some of them the death penalty ought to be replaced everywhere by imprisonment for life.

“I don’t agree with you,” said their host the banker. “I have not tried either the death penalty or imprisonment for life, but if one may judge a priori, the death penalty is more moral and more humane than imprisonment for life. Capital punishment kills a man at once, but lifelong imprisonment kills him slowly. Which executioner is the more humane, he who kills you in a few minutes or he who drags the life out of you in the course of many years?”

“Both are equally immoral,” observed one of the guests, “for they both have the same object⁠—to take away life. The State is not God. It has not the right to take away what it cannot restore when it wants to.”

Among the guests was a young lawyer, a young man of five-and-twenty. When he was asked his opinion, he said:

“The death sentence and the life sentence are equally immoral, but if I had to choose between the death penalty and imprisonment for life, I would certainly choose the second. To live anyhow is better than not at all.”

A lively discussion arose. The banker, who was younger and more nervous in those days, was suddenly carried away by excitement; he struck the table with his fist and shouted at the young man:

“It’s not true! I’ll bet you two millions you wouldn’t stay in solitary confinement for five years.”

“If you mean that in earnest,” said the young man, “I’ll take the bet, but I would stay not five but fifteen years.”

“Fifteen? Done!” cried the banker. “Gentlemen, I stake two millions!”

“Agreed! You stake your millions and I stake my freedom!” said the young man.

And this wild, senseless bet was carried out! The banker, spoilt and frivolous, with millions beyond his reckoning, was delighted at the bet. At supper he made fun of the young man, and said:

“Think better of it, young man, while there is still time. To me two millions are a trifle, but you are losing three or four of the best years of your life. I say three or four, because you won’t stay longer. Don’t forget either, you unhappy man, that voluntary confinement is a great deal harder to bear than compulsory. The thought that you have the right to step out in liberty at any moment will poison your whole existence in prison. I am sorry for you.”

And now the banker, walking to and fro, remembered all this, and asked himself: “What was the object of that bet? What is the good of that man’s losing fifteen years of his life and my throwing away two millions? Can it prove that the death penalty is better or worse than imprisonment for life? No, no. It was all nonsensical and meaningless. On my part it was the caprice of a pampered man, and on his part simple greed for money.⁠ ⁠…”

Then he remembered what followed that evening. It was decided that the young man should spend the years of his captivity under the strictest supervision in one of the lodges in the banker’s garden. It was agreed that for fifteen years he should not be free to cross the threshold of the lodge, to see human beings, to hear the human voice, or to receive letters and newspapers. He was allowed to have a musical instrument and books, and was allowed to write letters, to drink wine, and to smoke. By the terms of the agreement, the only relations he could have with the outer world were by a little window made purposely for that object. He might have anything he wanted⁠—books, music, wine, and so on⁠—in any quantity he desired by writing an order, but could only receive them through the window. The agreement provided for every detail and every trifle that would make his imprisonment strictly solitary, and bound the young man to stay there exactly fifteen years, beginning from twelve o’clock of November 14, 1870, and ending at twelve o’clock of November 14, 1885. The slightest attempt on his part to break the conditions, if only two minutes before the end, released the banker from the obligation to pay him two millions.

For the first year of his confinement, as far as one could judge from his brief notes, the prisoner suffered severely from loneliness and depression. The sounds of the piano could be heard continually day and night from his lodge. He refused wine and tobacco. Wine, he wrote, excites the desires, and desires are the worst foes of the prisoner; and besides, nothing could be more dreary than drinking good wine and seeing no one. And tobacco spoilt the air of his room. In the first year the books he sent for were principally of a light character; novels with a complicated love plot, sensational and fantastic stories, and so on.

In the second year the piano was silent in the lodge, and the prisoner asked only for the classics. In the fifth year music was audible again, and the prisoner asked for wine. Those who watched him through the window said that all that year he spent doing nothing but eating and drinking and lying on his bed, frequently yawning and angrily talking to himself. He did not read books. Sometimes at night he would sit down to write; he would spend hours writing, and in the morning tear up all that he had written. More than once he could be heard crying.

In the second half of the sixth year the prisoner began zealously studying languages, philosophy, and history. He threw himself eagerly into these studies⁠—so much so that the banker had enough to do to get him the books he ordered. In the course of four years some six hundred volumes were procured at his request. It was during this period that the banker received the following letter from his prisoner:

“My dear Jailer, I write you these lines in six languages. Show them to people who know the languages. Let them read them. If they find not one mistake I implore you to fire a shot in the garden. That shot will show me that my efforts have not been thrown away. The geniuses of all ages and of all lands speak different languages, but the same flame burns in them all. Oh, if you only knew what unearthly happiness my soul feels now from being able to understand them!” The prisoner’s desire was fulfilled. The banker ordered two shots to be fired in the garden.

Then after the tenth year, the prisoner sat immovably at the table and read nothing but the Gospel. It seemed strange to the banker that a man who in four years had mastered six hundred learned volumes should waste nearly a year over one thin book easy of comprehension. Theology and histories of religion followed the Gospels.

In the last two years of his confinement the prisoner read an immense quantity of books quite indiscriminately. At one time he was busy with the natural sciences, then he would ask for Byron or Shakespeare. There were notes in which he demanded at the same time books on chemistry, and a manual of medicine, and a novel, and some treatise on philosophy or theology. His reading suggested a man swimming in the sea among the wreckage of his ship, and trying to save his life by greedily clutching first at one spar and then at another.

II

The old banker remembered all this, and thought:

“Tomorrow at twelve o’clock he will regain his freedom. By our agreement I ought to pay him two millions. If I do pay him, it is all over with me: I shall be utterly ruined.”

masterNotes.context: Chekhov wrote "The Bet" in 1889, early in a career that would make him the most influential short-story writer of his generation, at a point when he was still writing quickly for periodicals and had not yet stepped back from his medical practice. The premise is a wager struck at a dinner party: a banker and a young lawyer argue over which is crueler, a life sentence or execution, and the argument hardens into an actual bet, with the lawyer volunteering to spend fifteen years in solitary confinement to prove his point. Chekhov returned constantly, across his career, to isolation, self-deception, and the gap between what people believe about themselves and what circumstance eventually reveals. Here he uses an almost fable-like premise less as a thought experiment than as a pressure chamber for testing two men against a single, artificial constraint over a very long stretch of time.
masterNotes.form: The story is told in brisk omniscient third person, compressing fifteen years into a few pages by cutting between the banker's present-tense anxiety on the final night and quick summaries of what filtered out of the lawyer's confinement year by year, glimpsed mostly through the books he requests. Chekhov gives almost no direct access to the lawyer's interior life during the wager itself; the reader learns what he has become only secondhand, through inference and a late document, which makes the ending depend on the reader's own interpretation rather than on being told how to feel. The structure narrows steadily toward a single scene, the banker's approach to the lodge, and the story's control of pace is an early, clear demonstration of restraint as technique.
keyImages: The banker's fist on the table and the two-million wager struck on the spot — the story's founding rash gesture, made at a dinner party over dessert.
The year-by-year list of what the prisoner requests to read, swinging from light novels to the classics to nothing at all.
The two gunshots the banker orders fired in the garden, confirming that the prisoner's six-language letter has passed muster.
The banker's present-tense arithmetic of ruin, which closes the excerpt mid-thought rather than resolving anything.
whatToNotice: Notice that the dinner-party argument stages two entirely abstract positions before either man has personally been tested by anything.
Notice how little direct speech the lawyer gets after his opening declaration — almost everything after is filtered through requests and rumor.
Notice the uneven pace of the year-by-year summary — the first year gets several sentences, other years barely a clause.
Notice how the six-language letter substitutes a document for any direct access to the prisoner's state of mind.
Notice the sequence of his reading — entertainment, then classics, then wine and idleness, then philosophy, then scripture, then everything at once — and what pattern that traces.
Notice that the excerpt ends on the banker doing arithmetic, not on any resolution of the wager.
discussionQuestions: The two men's opening positions are entirely abstract, argued before either has anything at stake. What does the story's method suggest is the danger of arguing that way?
Why might Chekhov give the reader the lawyer's reading list instead of his thoughts?
What does the swing in the prisoner's reading, from entertainment to scripture to everything at once, suggest about what years of isolation do to a mind?
Beyond this excerpt: the story eventually returns to the very argument that opened it, in a form neither man predicts. What, in this excerpt, would already complicate either man's original position?
furtherReading: Chekhov's *Ward No. 6* — a longer, darker treatment of confinement and the porous line between keeper and kept.
Fyodor Dostoevsky's *Notes from Underground* — an earlier Russian treatment of isolation chosen rather than imposed, useful for comparison of tone and conclusion.
The other stories in the same Standard Ebooks Constance Garnett collection, for tracing how Chekhov's method changed across a decade of story writing.

title: The Story of an Hour
author: Kate Chopin
text:
The Dream of an Hour

Knowing that Mrs. Mallard was afflicted with a heart trouble, great care was taken to break to her as gently as possible the news of her husband’s death.

It was her sister Josephine who told her, in broken sentences; veiled hints that revealed in half concealing. Her husband’s friend Richards was there, too, near her. It was he who had been in the newspaper office when intelligence of the railroad disaster was received, with Brently Mallard’s name leading the list of “killed.” He had only taken the time to assure himself of its truth by a second telegram, and had hastened to forestall any less careful, less tender friend in bearing the sad message.

She did not hear the story as many women have heard the same, with a paralyzed inability to accept its significance. She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment, in her sister’s arms. When the storm of grief had spent itself she went away to her room alone. She would have no one follow her.

There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair. Into this she sank, pressed down by a physical exhaustion that haunted her body and seemed to reach into her soul.

She could see in the open square before her house the tops of trees that where all aquiver with the new spring life. The delicious breath of rain was in the air. In the street below a peddler was crying his wares. The notes of a distant song which someone was singing reached her faintly, and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves.

There were patches of blue sky showing here and there through the clouds that had met and piled one above the other in the west facing her window.

She sat with her head thrown back upon the cushion of the chair, quite motionless, except when a sob came up into her throat and shook her, as a child who has cried itself to sleep continues to sob in its dreams.

She was young, with a fair, calm face, whose lines bespoke repression and even a certain strength. But now there was a dull stare in her eyes, whose gaze was fixed away off yonder on one of those patches of blue sky. It was not a glance of reflection, but rather indicated a suspension of intelligent thought.

There was something coming to her and she was waiting for it, fearfully. What was it? She did not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name. But she felt it creeping out of the sky, reaching toward her through the sounds, the scents, the color that filled the air.

Now her bosom rose and fell tumultuously. She was beginning to recognize this thing that was approaching to possess her, and she was striving to beat it back with her will⁠—as powerless as her two white slender hands would have been.

When she abandoned herself a little whispered word escaped her slightly parted lips. She said it over and over under her breath: “free, free, free!” The vacant stare and the look of terror that had followed it went from her eyes. They stayed keen and bright. Her pulses beat fast, and the coursing blood warmed and relaxed every inch of her body.

She did not stop to ask if it were or were not a monstrous joy that held her. A clear and exalted perception enabled her to dismiss the suggestion as trivial.

She knew that she would weep again when she saw the kind, tender hands folded in death; the face that had never looked save with love upon her, fixed and gray and dead. But she saw beyond that bitter moment a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely. And she opened and spread her arms out to them in welcome.

There would be no one to live for during those coming years; she would live for herself. There would be no powerful will bending hers in that blind persistence with which men and women believe they have a right to impose a private will upon a fellow creature. A kind intention or a cruel intention made the act seem no less a crime as she looked upon it in that brief moment of illumination.

And yet she had loved him⁠—sometimes. Often she had not. What did it matter? What could love, the unsolved mystery, count for in face of this possession of self-assertion which she suddenly recognized as the strongest impulse of her being!

“Free! Body and soul free!” she kept whispering.

Josephine was kneeling before the closed door with her lips to the keyhole, imploring for admission. “Louise, open the door! I beg; open the door⁠—you will make yourself ill. What are you doing, Louise? For heaven’s sake open the door.”

“Go away. I am not making myself ill.” No; she was drinking in a very elixir of life through that open window.

How fancy was running riot along those days ahead of her. Spring days, and summer days, and all sorts of days that would be her own. She breathed a quick prayer that life might be long. It was only yesterday she had thought with a shudder that life might be long, and now what a change.

She arose at length and opened the door to her sister’s importunities. There was a feverish triumph in her eyes, and she carried herself unwittingly like the goddess of Victory. She clasped her sister’s waist, and together they descended the stairs. Richard stood waiting for them at the bottom.

Someone was opening the front door with a latch key. It was Brently Mallard who entered, a little travel-stained, composedly carrying his gripsack and umbrella. He had been far from the scene of accident, and did not even know there had been one. He stood amazed at Josephine’s piercing cry; at Richard’s quick motion to screen him from the view of his wife, who just then looked up.

But Richard was too late.

When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease⁠—of joy that kills.

masterNotes.context: Kate Chopin wrote "The Story of an Hour" in April 1894, by her own account in a single sitting, at a point when she had already published a novel and was building a reputation through short fiction placed in national magazines. It appeared first in Vogue that December under the title "The Dream of an Hour," a magazine whose readers skewed toward exactly the kind of comfortable, married women the story addresses. Chopin was writing in St. Louis some years after her husband's death had left her, unusually for the period, both a widow and financially independent, and her fiction returned often to the private interior of women's married lives, a subject American magazine fiction rarely treated without moralizing. The story runs only a few pages, and that compression is deliberate: Chopin allows herself almost no room for a slow build.
masterNotes.form: Told in close third person centered on Louise Mallard, the story is organized around a single hour, opening with news delivered to her and closing before that hour has fully elapsed. Chopin uses short paragraphs and a restrained, almost clinical narrating voice for material that is anything but clinical, letting the gap between tone and content do much of the work. The middle section shifts from external event into an extended interior passage that follows a feeling arriving in Louise before she has language for it — the narration tracks sensation first and supplies the word only afterward, a sequencing that mirrors how the feeling overtakes her. The story's final turn depends on ironic structure rather than plot mechanics, and rereading it changes what every earlier sentence seems to mean.
keyImages: The open window Louise sits before after the news arrives, and the ordinary spring scene beyond it — treetops, peddler's cries, patches of blue sky — deliberately full of life at a moment the story marks as about death.
The description of Louise's body in the armchair, given as pure physical sensation before the story tells us anything about what she is feeling.
A single recurring word arriving in the interior passage before Louise can consciously admit it to herself.
The staircase and the door in the story's closing scene, staged with an almost theatrical precision.
whatToNotice: Notice exactly where the narration names Louise's feeling versus where it only describes physical sensation — track the lag between body and word.
Notice how much natural, springtime imagery is packed into a story ostensibly about grief, and ask what work that imagery is doing.
Notice the story's use of interruption — how often a thought or sentence is cut off mid-course in the interior section.
Notice how briskly the opening paragraph moves through the delivery of the news itself, compared to how slowly the story lingers afterward.
Notice the very last paragraph's clinical, detached diction, and how sharply it contrasts with everything the reader now knows.
discussionQuestions: Chopin gives the reader access to Louise's interior life but almost none to anyone else's. What does the story lose, or gain, by that imbalance?
How does the story's tight time frame, a single hour, shape what Chopin is able to do with irony that a longer span wouldn't allow?
The story never states outright what kind of marriage the Mallards had. What details does Chopin give the reader to work with instead?
Is the ending a judgment on marriage in general, on this particular marriage, or on something else altogether?
furtherReading: Chopin's *The Awakening* — a novel-length treatment of the same tension between a woman's inner life and the social role of wife.
Charlotte Perkins Gilman's "The Yellow Wallpaper" — a near-contemporary American story using a woman's confined interior state to comparable, though very differently paced, effect.
Per Seyersted's *Kate Chopin: A Critical Biography* — background on the magazine culture Chopin was writing into.

masterNotes.context: Clifton published "won't you celebrate with me" in *The Book of Light* (1993), well into a career that had already produced more than a dozen collections and two National Book Award nominations before she won the award outright in 2000. She grew up in Depew, New York, the descendant of a family who had preserved an oral history reaching back to an enslaved ancestor, and Clifton wrote often, though rarely directly, out of that inheritance. Her poems are almost never capitalized and use minimal punctuation, a signature style she maintained across four decades. This poem addresses the reader directly, asking for celebration rather than sympathy, and it has become one of her most frequently taught poems, especially for how plainly it names the specific conditions — race, gender, lack of precedent — that shaped the life it describes.
masterNotes.form: The poem is built as unrhymed, unpunctuated free verse, with even the personal pronoun "i" kept lowercase — Clifton refuses grammatical convention its usual deference throughout her work. A central image compresses the poem's argument about self-invention into a handful of words, comparing the space the speaker has made a life in to a bridge between two very different registers, the exalted and the ordinary. The poem builds toward its ending through direct address and accumulating clauses rather than metaphor, and its final short statement lands harder for arriving without any rhetorical flourish to cushion it.
keyImages: The poem naming its own starting conditions — birth into a hostile environment, and both a racial and gender identity that offered no ready model — without complaint or elaboration.
The central bridge image, self-invention pictured as a precarious position between the exalted and the ordinary.
A closing gesture of self-sufficiency, one hand holding the other, pictured as a literal, almost defiant, physical act.
whatToNotice: Notice the lowercase style throughout — even the poem's one first-person pronoun refuses standard capitalization.
Notice the poem is framed as an invitation to celebrate, rather than as a statement seeking sympathy.
Notice how flatly the final statement is delivered — no exclamation, just plain assertion.
Notice that place names and proper nouns are also kept lowercase, treated as conditions rather than as specific, capitalized places.
discussionQuestions: What is the effect of framing survival as something to celebrate rather than simply endure?
Why might Clifton refuse capitalization throughout, including on the first-person pronoun?
What does the bridge image suggest about how the speaker understands her own life?
furtherReading: "homage to my hips" (Clifton) — for the same unapologetic, plainspoken celebration of self in a different register.
*Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems* (Clifton) — the National Book Award–winning collection spanning her career.

title: Because I could not stop for Death
author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Because I could not stop for Death –
He kindly stopped for me –
The Carriage held but just Ourselves –
And Immortality.

We slowly drove – He knew no haste
And I had put away
My labor and my leisure too,
For His Civility –

We passed the School, where Children strove
At Recess – in the Ring –
We passed the Fields of Gazing Grain –
We passed the Setting Sun –

Or rather – He passed us –
The Dews drew quivering and Chill –
For only Gossamer, my Gown –
My Tippet – only Tulle –

We paused before a House that seemed
A Swelling of the Ground –
The Roof was scarcely visible –
The Cornice – in the Ground –

Since then – 'tis Centuries – and yet
Feels shorter than the Day
I first surmised the Horses' Heads
Were toward Eternity –

externalLinks.label: Search Poetry Foundation for this poem

masterNotes.context:
Dickinson wrote this poem in 1863 — Ralph Franklin's variorum numbers it 479, Thomas Johnson's earlier edition 712, and the two numbering systems are the reason the poem sometimes travels under different reference numbers in criticism. It was not published until 1890, four years after her death, when her editors gathered loose manuscripts into the first posthumous *Poems*. She lived a famously withdrawn life in Amherst, Massachusetts, and death was one of her most persistent subjects, staged again and again as an encounter rather than an abstraction.

The poem takes the New England custom of a horse-drawn funeral carriage and turns it into an unhurried social call: Death arrives not as a violent interruption but as a courteous suitor, and the speaker, mid-errand, simply goes along for the ride.
masterNotes.form:
The poem is written in Dickinson's signature common meter (alternating four- and three-stress lines), the meter of hymns and ballads, which lends even her most unsettling ideas a deceptively singable, familiar rhythm. Her characteristic dashes replace conventional punctuation throughout, creating pauses that feel like held breath rather than grammatical stops.

Slant rhyme ("me"/"Immortality," "Ground"/"Ground") and the slow widening of stanza scope — from carriage, to schoolyard, to fields, to sunset, to grave — build a quiet deceleration that mirrors the ride itself.
keyImages: The carriage holding "just Ourselves – / And Immortality" — a third, abstract passenger riding along as if it were a person.
The house that "seemed / A Swelling of the Ground" — the grave described with the softened, domestic word "House."
The final image of the horses' heads pointed "toward Eternity," left suspended without arrival.
whatToNotice: Death is personified as courteous and unhurried ("He kindly stopped for me"), never menacing — notice how that tone shapes your own sense of dread, or lack of it.
The speaker's clothing ("Gossamer," "Tulle") is unfit for the cold, marking the crossing from the world of the living into something else without ever naming it directly.
Time collapses in the final stanza: centuries feel shorter than the single day of the ride. Notice how the poem never actually arrives anywhere — it ends suspended, mid-journey.
The dashes control pacing more than grammar does. Try reading a stanza aloud, pausing only where a dash falls.
Notice the third stanza's triple anaphora, "We passed... We passed... We passed..." — a steady procession that stops abruptly when the syntax flips in the next line: "Or rather – He passed us."
discussionQuestions: Why might Dickinson have chosen to make Death a polite, familiar figure rather than a frightening one?
What is the effect of ending the poem mid-journey, with the horses still "toward Eternity," rather than at a clear arrival?
How does the hymn-like meter interact with the poem's subject? Does the familiarity of the rhythm comfort, unsettle, or both?
The speaker says she "could not stop for Death" — what does it change that Death, not the speaker, controls the pace of the whole ride?
furtherReading: Helen Vendler, *Dickinson: Selected Poems and Commentaries* — a close-reading companion covering this poem in detail.
[Poetry Foundation: Emily Dickinson](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/emily-dickinson) — biography and further poems.
"I'm Nobody! Who are you?" (Dickinson) — for the same dash-driven meter turned toward a much lighter subject.

title: Death, be not proud (Holy Sonnet X)
author: John Donne
text:
Death, be not proud, though some have called thee
Mighty and dreadful, for thou art not so;
For those, whom thou think’st thou dost overthrow,
Die not, poor Death, nor yet canst thou kill me.
From rest and sleep, which but thy picture be,
Much pleasure, then from thee much more must flow,
And soonest our best men with thee do go,
Rest of their bones, and soul’s delivery.
Thou’rt slave to Fate, chance, kings, and desperate men,
And dost with poison, war, and sickness dwell,
And poppy, or charms can make us sleep as well,
And better than thy stroke; why swell’st thou then?
One short sleep past, we wake eternally,
And Death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die.

masterNotes.context: Donne wrote his Holy Sonnets, this one among them, around 1609–1610, in the years after he had abandoned an early ambition for court advancement and before he was ordained in the Church of England in 1615. He circulated them privately in manuscript; they were not printed until 1633, two years after his death, in the first collected edition of his *Poems*. This sonnet is conventionally numbered the tenth in that sequence, following the ordering long used in anthologies and classrooms. Donne had lived through serious illness and the deaths of several close family members by the time he wrote it, and the poem reads less like a settled theological position than an argument the speaker is actively working himself into believing, sentence by sentence, in real time.
masterNotes.form: The poem is a direct address to a personified Death, structured as a single sustained argument across an Italian (Petrarchan) sonnet form, though Donne bends its octave/sestet logic to his own rhetorical needs. Each quatrain supplies a fresh reason Death has been overrated — a rest that resembles sleep, a servant to other, greater forces, a mere passage rather than an end — building toward the famous closing paradox, a final couplet that inverts the sonnet's addressee from feared power to condemned prisoner. The argumentative, almost legalistic momentum, characteristic of the metaphysical style, matters more here than any single image: the poem enacts persuasion rather than simply stating a conclusion.
keyImages: Death addressed directly as a person the speaker can rebuke to its face, sustained across all fourteen lines rather than dropped after an opening apostrophe.
Death likened to rest and sleep, images the poem treats as pleasurable rather than fearsome, undercutting Death's claim to being anything worse than a nap.
Death recast as a servant of larger forces — chance, kings, and desperate men — stripping it of independent power rather than granting it any.
The closing paradox in which Death itself is said to die, the poem's rhetorical payoff after thirteen lines of buildup.
whatToNotice: Notice that the poem opens by forbidding Death an emotion, pride, before it has offered a single argument — the rebuke comes first, the reasoning after.
Track how each quatrain adds one more argument rather than repeating the first; the poem accumulates its case instead of restating it.
Notice how often the poem compares Death to something ordinary and survivable, rather than describing Death's own terrors.
Watch the final couplet's grammar carefully — the poem's whole argument is compressed into a single reversal of subject and object.
Notice the sonnet never claims the speaker isn't afraid; it stages an argument against fear rather than an absence of it.
discussionQuestions: Is the speaker fully convinced by his own argument, or does the poem's insistence suggest he is still working to persuade himself?
What is the effect of addressing Death directly, in the second person, rather than describing it from a distance?
How does comparing Death to sleep change the emotional register of the poem compared to more conventional images of Death as a reaper or destroyer?
Does the poem's confidence depend on its Christian framework, or could a reader without that belief still find the argument persuasive on its own terms?
furtherReading: Donne's other Holy Sonnets (e.g. "Batter my heart, three-personed God") — for the same argumentative intensity turned toward a pleading rather than defiant address.
John Donne, sermon "Death's Duel" — his final sermon, delivered while visibly dying, on a related but far darker view of mortality.
Helen Gardner (ed.), *The Divine Poems of John Donne* — the standard scholarly edition and textual history of this sequence.

title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
author: Frederick Douglass
excerpt:
What to the American slave is your Fourth of July? I answer, a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim. To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity; your sounds of rejoicing are empty and heartless; your denunciations of tyrants, brass-fronted impudence; your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery; your prayers and hymns, your sermons and thanksgivings, with all your religious parade and solemnity,{353} are to him mere bombast, fraud, deception, impiety, and hypocrisy--a thin veil to cover up crimes which would disgrace a nation of savages. There is not a nation on the earth guilty of practices more shocking and bloody, than are the people of these United States, at this very hour.

Go where you may, search where you will, roam through all the monarchies and despotisms of the old world, travel through South America, search out every abuse, and when you have found the last, lay your facts by the side of the every-day practices of this nation, and you will say with me, that, for revolting barbarity and shameless hypocrisy, America reigns without a rival.

THE INTERNAL SLAVE TRADE. Extract from an Oration, at Rochester, July 5, 1852

Take the American slave trade, which, we are told by the papers, is especially prosperous just now. Ex-senator Benton tells us that the price of men was never higher than now. He mentions the fact to show that slavery is in no danger. This trade is one of the peculiarities of American institutions. It is carried on in all the large towns and cities in one-half of this confederacy; and millions are pocketed every year by dealers in this horrid traffic. In several states this trade is a chief source of wealth. It is called (in contradistinction to the foreign slave trade) _"the internal slave trade_." It is, probably, called so, too, in order to divert from it the horror with which the foreign slave trade is contemplated. That trade has long since been denounced by this government as piracy. It has been denounced with burning words, from the high places of the nation, as an execrable traffic. To arrest it, to put an end to it, this nation keeps a squadron, at immense cost, on the coast of Africa. Everywhere in this country, it is safe to speak of this foreign slave trade as a most inhuman traffic, opposed alike to the laws of God and of man. The duty to extirpate and destroy it is admitted even by our _doctors of divinity_. In order to put an end to it, some of these last have consented that their colored brethren (nominally free) should leave this country, and establish themselves on the western coast of Africa. It is, however, a notable fact, that, while so much execration is poured out by Americans, upon those engaged in the foreign slave trade, the men engaged in the slave trade between the states pass without condemnation, and their business is deemed honorable.

Behold the practical operation of this internal slave trade--the American slave trade sustained by American politics and American religion! Here you will see men and women reared like swine for the market. You know what is a swine-drover? I will show you a man-drover. They inhabit all our southern states. They perambulate the country, and crowd the{355} highways of the nation with droves of human stock. You will see one of these human-flesh-jobbers, armed with pistol, whip, and bowie-knife, driving a company of a hundred men, women, and children, from the Potomac to the slave market at New Orleans. These wretched people are to be sold singly, or in lots, to suit purchasers. They are food for the cotton-field and the deadly sugar-mill. Mark the sad procession as it moves wearily along, and the inhuman wretch who drives them. Hear his savage yells and his blood-chilling oaths, as he hurries on his affrighted captives. There, see the old man, with locks thinned and gray. Cast one glance, if you please, upon that young mother, whose shoulders are bare to the scorching sun, her briny tears falling on the brow of the babe in her arms. See, too, that girl of thirteen, weeping, yes, weeping, as she thinks of the mother from whom she has been torn. The drove moves tardily. Heat and sorrow have nearly consumed their strength. Suddenly you hear a quick snap, like the discharge of a rifle; the fetters clank, and the chain rattles simultaneously; your ears are saluted with a scream that seems to have torn its way to the center of your soul. The crack you heard was the sound of the slave whip; the scream you heard was from the woman you saw with the babe. Her speed had faltered under the weight of her child and her chains; that gash on her shoulder tells her to move on. Follow this drove to New Orleans. Attend the auction; see men examined like horses; see the forms of women rudely and brutally exposed to the shocking gaze of American slave-buyers. See this drove sold and separated forever; and never forget the deep, sad sobs that arose from that scattered multitude. Tell me, citizens, where, under the sun, can you witness a spectacle more fiendish and shocking. Yet this is but a glance at the American slave trade, as it exists at this moment, in the ruling part of the United States.

I was born amid such sights and scenes. To me the American slave trade is a terrible reality. When a child, my soul was often pierced with a sense of its horrors. I lived on Philpot street, Fell's Point, Baltimore, and have watched from the wharves the slave ships in the basin, anchored from the shore, with their cargoes of human flesh, waiting for favorable winds to waft them down the Chesapeake. There was, at that time, a grand slave mart kept at the head of Pratt street, by Austin Woldfolk. His agents were sent into every town and county in Maryland, announcing their arrival through the papers, and on flaming hand-bills, headed, "cash for negroes." These men were generally well dressed, and very captivating in their manners; ever ready to drink, to treat, and to gamble. The fate{356} of many a slave has depended upon the turn of a single card; and many a child has been snatched from the arms of its mothers by bargains arranged in a state of brutal drunkenness.

The flesh-mongers gather up their victims by dozens, and drive them, chained, to the general depot at Baltimore. When a sufficient number have been collected here, a ship is chartered, for the purpose of conveying the forlorn crew to Mobile or to New Orleans. From the slave-prison to the ship, they are usually driven in the darkness of night; for since the anti-slavery agitation a certain caution is observed.

In the deep, still darkness of midnight, I have been often aroused by the dead, heavy footsteps and the piteous cries of the chained gangs that passed our door. The anguish of my boyish heart was intense; and I was often consoled, when speaking to my mistress in the morning, to hear her say that the custom was very wicked; that she hated to hear the rattle of the chains, and the heart-rending cries. I was glad to find one who sympathized with me in my horror.

Fellow citizens, this murderous traffic is to-day in active operation in this boasted republic. In the solitude of my spirit, I see clouds of dust raised on the highways of the south; I see the bleeding footsteps; I hear the doleful wail of fettered humanity, on the way to the slave markets, where the victims are to be sold like horses, sheep, and swine, knocked off to the highest bidder. There I see the tenderest ties ruthlessly broken, to gratify the lust, caprice, and rapacity of the buyers and sellers of men. My soul sickens at the sight.

_Is this the land your fathers loved?
The freedom which they toiled to win?
Is this the earth whereon they moved?
Are these the graves they slumber in?_

masterNotes.context: Douglass delivered this address on July 5, 1852, at Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York, having accepted an invitation from the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society to speak at the city's Independence Day observance, deliberately scheduled a day after the actual holiday. Douglass, a formerly enslaved man who had become the era's most prominent Black abolitionist orator and editor, used the occasion to test what a national holiday of freedom could mean addressed to an audience that included people still legally enslaved elsewhere in the country. The speech was quickly printed as a pamphlet and remains one of the most anthologized pieces of American oratory, still read aloud publicly around the Fourth of July. The passage given here comes from partway through the address, at the point where Douglass turns the day's meaning directly onto the people listening to him.
masterNotes.form: Douglass builds this passage on classical rhetorical technique, direct address, escalating repetition, and rhetorical questions that require no answer because the answer is already implied. Having spent earlier portions of the speech establishing common ground and even praising the nation's founders, he pivots here into second person, separating himself and the audience by pronoun before separating them by argument. The effect is cumulative: each repeated phrase narrows the distance between celebration and accusation, so that by the passage's end the holiday itself has been redefined without any single explicit thesis statement announcing the turn.
keyImages: The repeated second-person address, "you" and "your," used to hold the holiday at arm's length from the speaker and, implicitly, from anyone still enslaved.
The catalog of the day's own rituals, prayers and hymns, sermons and thanksgivings, religious parade and solemnity, each one named only to be dismissed in the same breath as bombast and fraud.
The rhetorical question format itself, posed again and again so that the audience is made to supply an answer Douglass never states outright.
The turn from earlier praise of the nation's founding generation to a direct challenge aimed at the generation now listening to him.
whatToNotice: Notice the shift into second person, you and your, and how that pronoun choice positions Douglass outside the holiday he is describing.
Notice how each rhetorical question builds on the one before it, narrowing rather than repeating the same point.
Notice that Douglass never directly states his conclusion here, letting the accumulation of questions carry the argument instead.
Notice the contrast this passage draws between public patriotic display and private, unheard experience.
Notice how formal and controlled the sentence structure remains even as the accusation intensifies.
discussionQuestions: Why might Douglass choose escalating rhetorical questions rather than a single direct statement to make this argument?
What effect does the shift into second person have on an audience that considers itself the intended celebrants of the holiday?
How does irony function here as argument rather than as ornament?
Beyond this excerpt: given how sharply this passage turns the day's meaning back on its listeners, how might the speech's tone need to change again before it can close?
furtherReading: Douglass's *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass* — his own account of enslavement underlying the authority of this address.
David W. Blight's *Frederick Douglass: Prophet of Freedom* — a Pulitzer-winning biography with extensive treatment of this speech's composition and reception.
James Baldwin's essays on American racial hypocrisy — a later writer working a related rhetorical vein of turned national self-image.

title: We Wear the Mask
author: Paul Laurence Dunbar

source.name: Paul Laurence Dunbar, Majors and Minors (1895)

text:
We wear the mask that grins and lies,
It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,—
This debt we pay to human guile;
With torn and bleeding hearts we smile,
And mouth with myriad subtleties.

Why should the world be over-wise,
In counting all our tears and sighs?
Nay, let them only see us, while
      We wear the mask.

We smile, but, O great Christ, our cries
To thee from tortured souls arise.
We sing, but oh the clay is vile
Beneath our feet, and long the mile;
But let the world dream otherwise,
      We wear the mask!

externalLinks.label: Search Poetry Foundation for this poem

masterNotes.context: Dunbar published "We Wear the Mask" in 1895, in the collection *Majors and Minors*, three decades after the end of slavery and squarely within the era of Jim Crow segregation and the rollback of Reconstruction-era rights. He was the first African American poet to achieve a major national literary reputation, praised by William Dean Howells, though Howells's introduction to Dunbar's next book pushed him toward dialect poems at the expense of the formal, standard-English verse this poem represents — a tension Dunbar resented throughout his career. "We Wear the Mask" is written in that formal register, a rondeau borrowed from French verse tradition, and it speaks in a collective "we" rather than through a single character. It remains one of the most frequently taught and anthologized poems about the psychological cost of concealment under oppression.
masterNotes.form: The poem is a rondeau, a French form built on a refrain — "We wear the mask" — that closes each stanza and returns, slightly altered, as the poem's final words. That formal borrowing matters: Dunbar shows complete command of a demanding European verse form while writing about a mask forced onto Black Americans by a white audience unwilling to see past it. The poem's central irony sits in its own performance — a poem about hidden suffering that is itself formally poised and controlled, never breaking into the "torn and bleeding" register it describes. The direct address to "great Christ" in the final stanza is the poem's one break from its outward composure, a private cry the mask is explicitly not meant to show.
keyImages: "The mask that grins and lies" — a face deliberately built to perform an emotion it does not feel.
"With torn and bleeding hearts we smile" — the poem's central juxtaposition, agony and pleasant expression forced into the same line.
"O great Christ, our cries / To thee from tortured souls arise" — the one moment the mask is explicitly dropped, and only toward heaven, not toward the world.
whatToNotice: Notice the poem is spoken in "we," never "I" — the mask belongs to a whole community, not a single speaker.
Notice how formally controlled the poem's own language is, even while describing torn hearts and tortured souls.
Notice where the refrain "We wear the mask" falls in each stanza, and how its meaning shifts by the final exclamation point.
Notice that the poem never shows us what is underneath the mask directly — only that something is.
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that the poem's one moment of unmasked feeling is addressed to Christ rather than to the reader?
Why might Dunbar have chosen a tightly formal French verse structure to write about concealment and pain?
Does the collective "we" make the poem's argument more powerful, or does it flatten individual experience?
The poem twice tells "the world" what it is allowed to see. Who is that address really aimed at, and where do you, as the poem's actual reader, stand in relation to it?
furtherReading: Dunbar's dialect poems (e.g. "When Malindy Sings") — for the contrasting register Dunbar was pushed toward and sometimes resisted.
Paul Laurence Dunbar, *Lyrics of Lowly Life* — the 1896 collection that made this poem widely known.

title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
author: T. S. Eliot
form: dramatic monologue, free verse with intermittent rhyme
text:
Let us go then, you and I,
When the evening is spread out against the sky
Like a patient etherized upon a table;
Let us go, through certain half-deserted streets,
The muttering retreats
Of restless nights in one-night cheap hotels
And sawdust restaurants with oyster-shells:
Streets that follow like a tedious argument
Of insidious intent
To lead you to an overwhelming question.⁠ ⁠…
Oh, do not ask, “What is it?”
Let us go and make our visit.

In the room the women come and go
Talking of Michelangelo.

The yellow fog that rubs its back upon the windowpanes,
The yellow smoke that rubs its muzzle on the windowpanes
Licked its tongue into the corners of the evening,
Lingered upon the pools that stand in drains,
Let fall upon its back the soot that falls from chimneys,
Slipped by the terrace, made a sudden leap,
And seeing that it was a soft October night,
Curled once about the house, and fell asleep.

And indeed there will be time
For the yellow smoke that slides along the street,
Rubbing its back upon the window panes;
There will be time, there will be time
To prepare a face to meet the faces that you meet
There will be time to murder and create,
And time for all the works and days of hands
That lift and drop a question on your plate;
Time for you and time for me,
And time yet for a hundred indecisions,
And for a hundred visions and revisions,
Before the taking of a toast and tea.

In the room the women come and go
Talking of Michelangelo.

And indeed there will be time
To wonder, “Do I dare?” and, “Do I dare?”
Time to turn back and descend the stair,
With a bald spot in the middle of my hair⁠—
(They will say: “How his hair is growing thin!”)
My morning coat, my collar mounting firmly to the chin,
My necktie rich and modest, but asserted by a simple pin⁠—
(They will say: “But how his arms and legs are thin!”)
Do I dare
Disturb the universe?
In a minute there is time
For decisions and revisions which a minute will reverse.

For I have known them all already, known them all:
Have known the evenings, mornings, afternoons,
I have measured out my life with coffee spoons;
I know the voices dying with a dying fall
Beneath the music from a farther room.
So how should I presume?

And I have known the eyes already, known them all⁠—
The eyes that fix you in a formulated phrase,
And when I am formulated, sprawling on a pin,
When I am pinned and wriggling on the wall,
Then how should I begin
To spit out all the butt-ends of my days and ways?
And how should I presume?

And I have known the arms already, known them all⁠—
Arms that are braceleted and white and bare
(But in the lamplight, downed with light brown hair!)
Is it perfume from a dress
That makes me so digress?
Arms that lie along a table, or wrap about a shawl.
And should I then presume?
And how should I begin?

Shall I say, I have gone at dusk through narrow streets
And watched the smoke that rises from the pipes
Of lonely men in shirtsleeves, leaning out of windows?⁠ ⁠…

I should have been a pair of ragged claws
Scuttling across the floors of silent seas.

And the afternoon, the evening, sleeps so peacefully!
Smoothed by long fingers,
Asleep⁠ ⁠… tired⁠ ⁠… or it malingers.
Stretched on the floor, here beside you and me.
Should I, after tea and cakes and ices,
Have the strength to force the moment to its crisis?
But though I have wept and fasted, wept and prayed,
Though I have seen my head (grown slightly bald) brought in upon a platter,
I am no prophet⁠—and here’s no great matter;
I have seen the moment of my greatness flicker,
And I have seen the eternal Footman hold my coat, and snicker,
And in short, I was afraid.

And would it have been worth it, after all,
After the cups, the marmalade, the tea,
Among the porcelain, among some talk of you and me,
Would it have been worth while,
To have bitten off the matter with a smile,
To have squeezed the universe into a ball
To roll it toward some overwhelming question,
To say: “I am Lazarus, come from the dead,
Come back to tell you all, I shall tell you all”⁠—
If one, settling a pillow by her head,
Should say: “That is not what I meant at all;
That is not it, at all.”

And would it have been worth it, after all,
Would it have been worth while,
After the sunsets and the dooryards and the sprinkled streets,
After the novels, after the teacups, after the skirts that trail along the floor⁠—
And this, and so much more?⁠—
It is impossible to say just what I mean!
But as if a magic lantern threw the nerves in patterns on a screen:
Would it have been worth while
If one, settling a pillow or throwing off a shawl,
And turning toward the window, should say:
“That is not it at all,
That is not what I meant, at all.”

No! I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be;
Am an attendant lord, one that will do
To swell a progress, start a scene or two,
Advise the prince; no doubt, an easy tool,
Deferential, glad to be of use,
Politic, cautious, and meticulous;
Full of high sentence, but a bit obtuse;
At times, indeed, almost ridiculous⁠—
Almost, at times, the Fool.

I grow old⁠ ⁠… I grow old⁠ ⁠…
I shall wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled.

Shall I part my hair behind? Do I dare to eat a peach?
I shall wear white flannel trousers, and walk upon the beach.
I have heard the mermaids singing, each to each.

I do not think that they will sing to me.

I have seen them riding seaward on the waves
Combing the white hair of the waves blown back
When the wind blows the water white and black.

We have lingered in the chambers of the sea
By sea-girls wreathed with seaweed red and brown
Till human voices wake us, and we drown.
