masterNotes.context: Katherine Mansfield wrote "The Garden Party" in 1921 while living in France, already seriously ill with the tuberculosis that would kill her the following year, and it was first published in three installments in the Saturday Westminster Gazette in February 1922 before appearing that same year in the collection *The Garden Party and Other Stories*. Mansfield, born and raised in Wellington, New Zealand, drew on the house and social world of her own prosperous childhood there for the story's setting, one of several late stories in which she returned imaginatively to New Zealand after years of living in England and Europe. She is often grouped with the modernists for her interest in interior perception over plot mechanics, closer in method to Virginia Woolf, with whom she had a wary mutual respect, than to the more conventional short fiction being published in English magazines at the time.
masterNotes.form: The story is told in a close, mobile third person that drifts between the Sheridan family's viewpoints, settling for most of its length on Laura, the daughter whose perception the story is most interested in testing. Mansfield builds the story less through plot event than through texture — the arrangements for the party, the household's various voices and small frictions — before introducing a piece of outside information that reorients everything that follows. The prose moves quickly between registers, comic in the household scenes, suddenly still and exact once Laura's attention shifts elsewhere, and Mansfield trusts long stretches of sensory notation to carry thematic weight without the narration commenting on it directly. The structure withholds resolution in its closing lines, ending on an unfinished sentence rather than a stated conclusion.
keyImages: The marquee men debating where the tent should go, settling on a spot that will hide the karaka trees from view.
The tall workman pausing to pinch and smell a sprig of lavender — the gesture that unsettles Laura's sense of class distance.
The two small spots of sun playing on the inkpot and the photograph frame while Laura sits by the telephone.
The tray of pink canna lilies arriving at the door just as the excerpt ends — "nothing but lilies."
whatToNotice: Notice how early the marquee men arrive — before breakfast is even finished.
Notice Laura copying her mother's voice with the workmen, then stammering the moment it doesn't hold.
Notice what the lavender gesture specifically triggers in Laura's thinking about class, and how fast that thought arrives.
Notice the narration's move, mid-scene, from Laura's exchange outside straight into the house's internal sounds — the piano on its castors, doors swinging.
Notice the diction given to the sunspots on the inkpot, "darling little spots," and whose perception that phrase belongs to.
Notice that Mrs. Sheridan's instructions reach Laura only as a voice from upstairs, never in a scene of her own.
discussionQuestions: Laura insists she doesn't feel "these absurd class distinctions." Does the scene with the workmen support that claim or complicate it?
What does the lavender gesture do to Laura's view of the tall workman, and why might that particular detail be the one that lands?
Why might Mansfield give so much attention to small, ordinary sensations — sunspots, the smell of lavender — in a scene that's mostly logistics?
What has this excerpt trained you to notice, given that it ends the moment the lilies arrive?
Beyond this excerpt: the day's mood does not hold for the rest of the story. Rereading this excerpt, what in it, if anything, already hints that it might not?
furtherReading: Mansfield's "Miss Brill" — a shorter, quieter story sharing her interest in a single character's shifting perception.
Virginia Woolf's *Mrs Dalloway* — a near-contemporary novel built on a similar interest in a single day and the interior life beneath a social occasion.
Claire Tomalin's biography *Katherine Mansfield: A Secret Life* — for the New Zealand background behind the story's setting.

title: The Necklace
author: Guy de Maupassant
excerpt:
The Necklace

She was one of those pretty and charming girls born, as though fate had blundered over her, into a family of artisans. She had no marriage portion, no expectations, no means of getting known, understood, loved, and wedded by a man of wealth and distinction; and she let herself besides be married off to a little clerk in the Ministry of Education.

Her tastes were simple because she had never been able to afford any other, but she was as unhappy as though she had married beneath her; for women have no caste or class, their beauty, grace, and charm serving them for birth or family. Their natural delicacy, their instinctive elegance, their nimbleness of wit, are their only mark of rank, and put the slum girl on a level with the highest lady in the land.

She suffered endlessly, feeling herself born for every delicacy and luxury. She suffered from the poorness of her house, from its mean walls, worn chairs, and ugly curtains. All these things, of which other women of her class would not even have been aware, tormented and insulted her. The sight of the little Breton girl who came to do the work in her little house aroused heartbroken regrets and hopeless dreams in her mind. She imagined silent antechambers, heavy with Oriental tapestries, lit by torches in lofty bronze sockets, with two tall footmen in knee-breeches sleeping in large armchairs, overcome by the heavy warmth of the stove. She imagined vast saloons hung with antique silks, exquisite pieces of furniture supporting priceless ornaments, and small, charming, perfumed rooms, created just for little parties of intimate friends, men who were famous and sought after, whose homage roused every other woman’s envious longings.

When she sat down for dinner at the round table covered with a three-days-old cloth, opposite her husband, who took the cover off the soup tureen, exclaiming delightedly: “Aha! Scotch broth! There’s nothing better,” she imagined delicate meals, gleaming silver, tapestries peopling the walls with folk of a past age and strange birds in faery forests; she imagined delicate food served in marvellous dishes, murmured gallantries, listened to with an inscrutable smile as one trifled with the rosy flesh of trout or wings of asparagus chicken.

She had no clothes, no jewels, nothing. And these were the only things she loved; she felt that she was made for them. She had longed so eagerly to charm, to be desired, to be wildly attractive and sought after.

She had a rich friend, an old school friend whom she refused to visit, because she suffered so keenly when she returned home. She would weep whole days, with grief, regret, despair, and misery.

One evening her husband came home with an exultant air, holding a large envelope in his hand.

“Here’s something for you,” he said.

Swiftly she tore the paper and drew out a printed card on which were these words:

“The Minister of Education and Madame Ramponneau request the pleasure of the company of Monsieur and Madame Loisel at the Ministry on the evening of Monday, January the 18th.”

Instead of being delighted, as her husband hoped, she flung the invitation petulantly across the table, murmuring:

“What do you want me to do with this?”

“Why, darling, I thought you’d be pleased. You never go out, and this is a great occasion. I had tremendous trouble to get it. Everyone wants one; it’s very select, and very few go to the clerks. You’ll see all the really big people there.”

She looked at him out of furious eyes, and said impatiently:

“And what do you suppose I am to wear at such an affair?”

He had not thought about it; he stammered:

“Why, the dress you go to the theatre in. It looks very nice, to me.⁠ ⁠…”

He stopped, stupefied and utterly at a loss when he saw that his wife was beginning to cry. Two large tears ran slowly down from the corners of her eyes towards the corners of her mouth.

“What’s the matter with you? What’s the matter with you?” he faltered.

But with a violent effort she overcame her grief and replied in a calm voice, wiping her wet cheeks:

“Nothing. Only I haven’t a dress and so I can’t go to this party. Give your invitation to some friend of yours whose wife will be turned out better than I shall.”

He was heartbroken.

“Look here, Mathilde,” he persisted. “What would be the cost of a suitable dress, which you could use on other occasions as well, something very simple?”

She thought for several seconds, reckoning up prices and also wondering for how large a sum she could ask without bringing upon herself an immediate refusal and an exclamation of horror from the careful-minded clerk.

At last she replied with some hesitation:

“I don’t know exactly, but I think I could do it on four hundred francs.”

He grew slightly pale, for this was exactly the amount he had been saving for a gun, intending to get a little shooting next summer on the plain of Nanterre with some friends who went lark-shooting there on Sundays.

Nevertheless he said: “Very well. I’ll give you four hundred francs. But try and get a really nice dress with the money.”

The day of the party drew near, and Madame Loisel seemed sad, uneasy and anxious. Her dress was ready, however. One evening her husband said to her:

“What’s the matter with you? You’ve been very odd for the last three days.”

“I’m utterly miserable at not having any jewels, not a single stone, to wear,” she replied. “I shall look absolutely no one. I would almost rather not go to the party.”

“Wear flowers,” he said. “They’re very smart at this time of year. For ten francs you could get two or three gorgeous roses.”

She was not convinced.

“No⁠ ⁠… there’s nothing so humiliating as looking poor in the middle of a lot of rich women.”

“How stupid you are!” exclaimed her husband. “Go and see Madame Forestier and ask her to lend you some jewels. You know her quite well enough for that.”

She uttered a cry of delight.

“That’s true. I never thought of it.”

Next day she went to see her friend and told her her trouble.

Madame Forestier went to her dressing-table, took up a large box, brought it to Madame Loisel, opened it, and said:

“Choose, my dear.”

First she saw some bracelets, then a pearl necklace, then a Venetian cross in gold and gems, of exquisite workmanship. She tried the effect of the jewels before the mirror, hesitating, unable to make up her mind to leave them, to give them up. She kept on asking:

“Haven’t you anything else?”

“Yes. Look for yourself. I don’t know what you would like best.”

Suddenly she discovered, in a black satin case, a superb diamond necklace; her heart began to beat covetously. Her hands trembled as she lifted it. She fastened it round her neck, upon her high dress, and remained in ecstasy at sight of herself.

Then, with hesitation, she asked in anguish:

“Could you lend me this, just this alone?”

“Yes, of course.”

She flung herself on her friend’s breast, embraced her frenziedly, and went away with her treasure.

The day of the party arrived. Madame Loisel was a success. She was the prettiest woman present, elegant, graceful, smiling, and quite above herself with happiness. All the men stared at her, inquired her name, and asked to be introduced to her. All the undersecretaries of state were eager to waltz with her. The Minister noticed her.

She danced madly, ecstatically, drunk with pleasure, with no thought for anything, in the triumph of her beauty, in the pride of her success, in a cloud of happiness made up of this universal homage and admiration, of the desires she had aroused, of the completeness of a victory so dear to her feminine heart.

She left about four o’clock in the morning. Since midnight her husband had been dozing in a deserted little room, in company with three other men whose wives were having a good time.

He threw over her shoulders the garments he had brought for them to go home in, modest everyday clothes, whose poorness clashed with the beauty of the ball dress. She was conscious of this and was anxious to hurry away, so that she would not be noticed by the other women putting on their costly furs.

Loisel restrained her.

“Wait a little. You’ll catch cold in the open. I’m going to fetch a cab.”

But she did not listen to him and rapidly descended the staircase. When they were out in the street they could not find a cab; they began to look for one, shouting at the drivers whom they saw passing in the distance.

masterNotes.context: Guy de Maupassant published "The Necklace" ("La Parure") in the Paris newspaper Le Gaulois in February 1884, at the height of a decade in which he produced an enormous body of short fiction while working under Gustave Flaubert's early mentorship. The story belongs to a group of his Paris stories preoccupied with money, class position, and the gap between how people present themselves and what they can actually afford, a subject sharpened by his view of the anxious, status-conscious middle class of the Third Republic. It was collected the same year in *Contes du jour et de la nuit* and became one of his most reprinted and most taught stories, prized less for stylistic ornament than for the mechanical precision of its plotting — a quality that made it a standard example, for generations of writing students, of how a short story's structure can carry its meaning. The Standard Ebooks edition draws on several period English translations rather than a single named translator for every story in the collection.
masterNotes.form: Maupassant tells the story in close but slightly cool third person, tracking Mathilde Loisel's discontent in a compressed opening before the plot proper begins, so the reader understands her temperament fully before a single event tests it. The prose is plain and unornamented by design — Maupassant, trained by Flaubert to prize precision over embellishment, gives almost no scene more description than it needs to function, which makes the story's few extended set pieces stand out by contrast. The plot runs on a strict economy of cause and consequence, each decision Mathilde makes narrowing her options further, and the story's well-known final lines depend on the reader having tracked that chain of causation closely enough to feel its full weight land at once.
keyImages: The catalogue of Mathilde's shabby apartment — worn chairs, mean walls — laid out before a single event happens to her.
Her husband's small pleasure at the dinner-table soup, met by her private disgust in the very next sentence.
The four hundred francs redirected from her husband's planned gun purchase — an early, concrete price for her one evening.
The moment her hands tremble over the diamond necklace, singled out from an entire box of otherwise unremarkable jewels.
whatToNotice: Notice how many sentences the story spends imagining luxuries Mathilde doesn't have before anything actually happens to her.
Notice her husband's two proposed solutions, flowers and then the loan, and how differently each one lands.
Notice the exact sum of four hundred francs, and what it had already been earmarked for.
Notice how much longer the narration lingers on Mathilde trying on the necklace than on any other single object in the box.
Notice her mood at the party itself, "drunk with pleasure," set against the tone of every earlier paragraph.
Notice her urgency to leave before the other women see her plain coat, and her refusal to wait for her husband's cab.
discussionQuestions: Maupassant spends real narrative effort making Mathilde's dissatisfaction legible before the plot begins. Does this excerpt ask you to judge her for it, or something more complicated?
What does the husband's readiness to give up his gun money suggest about this marriage, this early on?
Why single out the diamond necklace for such a strong physical reaction, among an entire box of jewels?
Mathilde rushes to leave before the other women see her coat. What does that urgency suggest about what the evening has, and hasn't, changed in her?
furtherReading: Maupassant's "Boule de Suif" — a longer story sharing the same interest in how social class distorts individual judgment.
Anton Chekhov's short fiction, frequently compared to Maupassant's for its economy, though built on very different assumptions about plot.
W. Somerset Maugham's essays on the craft of the short story, which repeatedly cite Maupassant's plotting as a model of structural discipline.

title: Time does not bring relief; you all have lied
author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
text:
Time does not bring relief; you all have lied
Who told me time would ease me of my pain!
I miss him in the weeping of the rain;
I want him at the shrinking of the tide;
The old snows melt from every mountain-side,
And last year's leaves are smoke in every lane;
But last year's bitter loving must remain
Heaped on my heart, and my old thoughts abide!

There are a hundred places where I fear
To go,--so with his memory they brim!
And entering with relief some quiet place
Where never fell his foot or shone his face
I say, "There is no memory of him here!"
And so stand stricken, so remembering him!

masterNotes.context: Millay published this sonnet in 1917 in her first full collection, *Renascence and Other Poems*, released the same year she graduated from Vassar College, when she was twenty-five. The book made her reputation less on its title poem, an ambitious meditation on death and rebirth she had written as a teenager, than on a cluster of shorter lyrics and sonnets, this one among them, that showed a colder, more skeptical voice than the era's popular sentimental verse about grief. Millay would go on to become one of the most widely read American poets of the 1920s, celebrated for exactly this kind of formally traditional but emotionally blunt sonnet. The poem takes direct aim at a piece of common consolation, that time heals loss, and refuses it outright rather than easing into agreement.
masterNotes.form: The poem is a Petrarchan sonnet, its octave built almost entirely from a list of ordinary places and objects the speaker still cannot encounter without grief resurfacing, before the closing sestet turns from complaint to a sharper, more specific admission. Millay's diction throughout is plain and declarative rather than ornate, which sharpens the argument: this is a poem that wants to sound like blunt fact, not decorated feeling. The formal control of the sonnet, its steady meter and full rhymes, sits in deliberate tension with the raw claim being made inside it, so that composure and grief are made to occupy the same lines rather than one giving way to the other.
keyImages: The catalogue of ordinary, unremarkable places the speaker still cannot pass without being reminded of the loss — grief attached to geography rather than to any single dramatic scene.
The direct rebuttal of secondhand comfort in the opening line, the poem positioning itself against everyone else's reassurance before offering its own view.
The turn in the sestet toward a narrower, more physical admission of what the speaker still cannot do, sharpening the poem's abstract claim about grief into something concrete.
whatToNotice: Notice that the poem opens by contradicting other people's comfort rather than describing the loss itself — the argument comes before the grief is even named.
Notice how the octave accumulates ordinary settings rather than one big, dramatic scene of mourning.
Watch for the sonnet's turn between octave and sestet, and notice how the claim narrows rather than widens at that point.
Notice how plain and unadorned the diction stays throughout, even as the feeling being described is severe.
discussionQuestions: Why might Millay open by rejecting other people's comfort rather than describing her own grief first?
What is the effect of using a traditional, tightly rhymed sonnet form to make an argument against a comforting cliché?
Does the poem's insistence that time does not heal read as more true, or less, for being stated so flatly rather than dramatized?
How does moving from general claim (octave) to specific admission (sestet) change how convincing the poem feels by its final lines?
furtherReading: "Renascence" (Millay, same collection) — the volume's more famous title poem, for a very different, visionary treatment of death and survival.
Edna St. Vincent Millay, *A Few Figs from Thistles* (1920) — for the wittier, more defiant voice she became known for shortly after this collection.
Nancy Milford, *Savage Beauty: The Life of Edna St. Vincent Millay* — a biography covering the period of Millay's early sonnets.

title: Remember
author: Christina Rossetti

source.name: Christina Rossetti, Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862)

text:
Remember me when I am gone away,
   Gone far away into the silent land;
   When you can no more hold me by the hand,
Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay.
Remember me when no more day by day
   You tell me of our future that you plann'd:
   Only remember me; you understand
It will be late to counsel then or pray.
Yet if you should forget me for a while
   And afterwards remember, do not grieve:
   For if the darkness and corruption leave
A vestige of the thoughts that once I had,
   Better by far you should forget and smile
   Than that you should remember and be sad.

externalLinks.label: Search Poetry Foundation for this poem

masterNotes.context: Rossetti wrote "Remember" around 1849, when she was still a teenager, though it wasn't published until 1862 in her first major collection, *Goblin Market and Other Poems*. She was part of the Pre-Raphaelite circle through her brother Dante Gabriel Rossetti, but her own poetry is generally plainer and more devotional in temper than the movement's visual lushness. She never married, and a recurring subject across her work is renunciation — of love, of desire, of claims on another person — treated not as bitterness but as a kind of discipline. "Remember" imagines the speaker's own death and instructs a survivor on how to grieve, a fairly common Victorian poetic occasion, but the poem's turn in its final six lines, releasing the beloved from the very request it just made, is Rossetti's own.
masterNotes.form: The poem is a Petrarchan sonnet, split at the volta between octave and sestet exactly where its argument turns. The octave insists, three times, on the imperative "Remember," building an almost desperate repetition, before the sestet reverses course entirely: better to forget and smile than to remember and grieve. The rhyme scheme (abba abba cdd ece) is fairly conventional Petrarchan form, but the poem uses its meter's regularity to make the reversal land harder — nothing in the sound changes, only the argument does, so the shift feels like a decision rather than a collapse.
keyImages: "The silent land" — death rendered as a place rather than an ending, something the beloved is being sent toward rather than simply losing.
"Yet if you should forget me for a while / And afterwards remember" — the poem imagining its own request being ignored, and forgiving that in advance.
The closing antithesis, "forget and smile" against "remember and be sad" — the entire poem's argument compressed into one line.
whatToNotice: Count how many times "remember" appears in the octave before the sestet begins undoing the request.
Notice the poem never says how or when the speaker dies — only that the day will come.
Notice the sestet doesn't simply soften the request, it reverses it: better to be forgotten happily than remembered sadly.
Notice how little the poem's music changes at the volta — the reversal is entirely in the argument, not the sound.
discussionQuestions: Why might Rossetti have the speaker undo her own request rather than simply asking to be remembered?
What does the poem suggest about the relationship between love and self-effacement?
Is the sestet's offer to be forgotten a genuine release, or another, subtler way of asking to be remembered?
furtherReading: "Song" ("When I am dead, my dearest") — Rossetti's other, even starker poem on being forgotten after death.
*Goblin Market* (Rossetti) — for a very different register of the same poet's imagination, allegorical rather than devotional.

title: The Wonderful Adventures of Nils
author: Selma Lagerlöf
form: novel, translated from Swedish by Velma Swanston Howard
excerpt:
The Boy

The Elf

Sunday, March twentieth.

Once there was a boy. He was⁠—let us say⁠—something like fourteen years old; long and loose-jointed and towheaded. He wasn’t good for much, that boy. His chief delight was to eat and sleep; and after that⁠—he liked best to make mischief.

It was a Sunday morning and the boy’s parents were getting ready to go to church. The boy sat on the edge of the table, in his shirt sleeves, and thought how lucky it was that both father and mother were going away, and the coast would be clear for a couple of hours. “Good! Now I can take down pop’s gun and fire off a shot, without anybody’s meddling interference,” he said to himself.

But it was almost as if father should have guessed the boy’s thoughts, for just as he was on the threshold⁠—ready to start⁠—he stopped short, and turned toward the boy. “Since you won’t come to church with mother and me,” he said, “the least you can do, is to read the service at home. Will you promise to do so?”

“Yes,” said the boy, “that I can do easy enough.” And he thought, of course, that he wouldn’t read any more than he felt like reading.

The boy thought that never had he seen his mother so persistent. In a second she was over by the shelf near the fireplace, and took down Luther’s Commentary and laid it on the table, in front of the window⁠—opened at the service for the day. She also opened the New Testament, and placed it beside the Commentary. Finally, she drew up the big armchair, which was bought at the parish auction the year before, and which, as a rule, no one but father was permitted to occupy.

The boy sat thinking that his mother was giving herself altogether too much trouble with this spread; for he had no intention of reading more than a page or so. But now, for the second time, it was almost as if his father were able to see right through him. He walked up to the boy, and said in a severe tone: “Now, remember, that you are to read carefully! For when we come back, I shall question you thoroughly; and if you have skipped a single page, it will not go well with you.”

“The service is fourteen and a half pages long,” said his mother, just as if she wanted to heap up the measure of his misfortune. “You’ll have to sit down and begin the reading at once, if you expect to get through with it.”

With that they departed. And as the boy stood in the doorway watching them, he thought that he had been caught in a trap. “There they go congratulating themselves, I suppose, in the belief that they’ve hit upon something so good that I’ll be forced to sit and hang over the sermon the whole time that they are away,” thought he.

But his father and mother were certainly not congratulating themselves upon anything of the sort; but, on the contrary, they were very much distressed. They were poor farmers, and their place was not much bigger than a garden-plot. When they first moved there, the place couldn’t feed more than one pig and a pair of chickens; but they were uncommonly industrious and capable folk⁠—and now they had both cows and geese. Things had turned out very well for them; and they would have gone to church that beautiful morning⁠—satisfied and happy⁠—if they hadn’t had their son to think of. Father complained that he was dull and lazy; he had not cared to learn anything at school, and he was such an all-round good-for-nothing, that he could barely be made to tend geese. Mother did not deny that this was true; but she was most distressed because he was wild and bad; cruel to animals, and ill-willed toward human beings. “May God soften his hard heart, and give him a better disposition!” said the mother, “or else he will be a misfortune, both to himself and to us.”

The boy stood for a long time and pondered whether he should read the service or not. Finally, he came to the conclusion that, this time, it was best to be obedient. He seated himself in the easy chair, and began to read. But when he had been rattling away in an undertone for a little while, this mumbling seemed to have a soothing effect upon him⁠—and he began to nod.

It was the most beautiful weather outside! It was only the twentieth of March; but the boy lived in West Vemminghög Township, down in Southern Skåne, where the spring was already in full swing. It was not as yet green, but it was fresh and budding. There was water in all the trenches, and the colt’s-foot on the edge of the ditch was in bloom. All the weeds that grew in among the stones were brown and shiny. The beech-woods in the distance seemed to swell and grow thicker with every second. The skies were high⁠—and a clear blue. The cottage door stood ajar, and the lark’s trill could be heard in the room. The hens and geese pattered about in the yard, and the cows, who felt the spring air away in their stalls, lowed their approval every now and then.

The boy read and nodded and fought against drowsiness. “No! I don’t want to fall asleep,” thought he, “for then I’ll not get through with this thing the whole forenoon.”

But⁠—somehow⁠—he fell asleep.

He did not know whether he had slept a short while, or a long while; but he was awakened by hearing a slight noise back of him.

On the windowsill, facing the boy, stood a small looking-glass; and almost the entire cottage could be seen in this. As the boy raised his head, he happened to look in the glass; and then he saw that the cover to his mother’s chest had been opened.

His mother owned a great, heavy, iron-bound oak chest, which she permitted no one but herself to open. Here she treasured all the things she had inherited from her mother, and of these she was especially careful. Here lay a couple of old-time peasant dresses, of red homespun cloth, with short bodice and plaited shirt, and a pearl-bedecked breast pin. There were starched white-linen headdresses, and heavy silver ornaments and chains. Folks don’t care to go about dressed like that in these days, and several times his mother had thought of getting rid of the old things; but somehow, she hadn’t had the heart to do it.

Now the boy saw distinctly⁠—in the glass⁠—that the chest-lid was open. He could not understand how this had happened, for his mother had closed the chest before she went away. She never would have left that precious chest open when he was at home, alone.

He became low-spirited and apprehensive. He was afraid that a thief had sneaked his way into the cottage. He didn’t dare to move; but sat still and stared into the looking-glass.

While he sat there and waited for the thief to make his appearance, he began to wonder what that dark shadow was which fell across the edge of the chest. He looked and looked⁠—and did not want to believe his eyes. But the thing, which at first seemed shadowy, became more and more clear to him; and soon he saw that it was something real. It was no less a thing than an elf who sat there⁠—astride the edge of the chest!

To be sure, the boy had heard stories about elves, but he had never dreamed that they were such tiny creatures. He was no taller than a hand’s breadth⁠—this one, who sat on the edge of the chest. He had an old, wrinkled and beardless face, and was dressed in a black frock coat, knee-breeches and a broad-brimmed black hat. He was very trim and smart, with his white laces about the throat and wristbands, his buckled shoes, and the bows on his garters. He had taken from the chest an embroidered piece, and sat and looked at the old-fashioned handiwork with such an air of veneration, that he did not observe the boy had awakened.

The boy was somewhat surprised to see the elf, but, on the other hand, he was not particularly frightened. It was impossible to be afraid of one who was so little. And since the elf was so absorbed in his own thoughts that he neither saw nor heard, the boy thought that it would be great fun to play a trick on him; to push him over into the chest and shut the lid on him, or something of that kind.

masterNotes.context: Lagerlöf wrote *The Wonderful Adventures of Nils* on commission from the National Teachers' Association of Sweden, which wanted an engaging geography reader for schoolchildren; she answered the brief by sending a shrunken, disobedient boy flying the length of the country on the back of a farm goose, folding real regional landscape, wildlife, and folklore into a continuous adventure rather than a textbook. Published in two volumes in 1906 and 1907, it became her best-known work internationally and helped bring her the 1909 Nobel Prize in Literature, making her the first woman to receive it. Velma Swanston Howard's English translation, prepared soon after, was for decades the version through which Anglophone readers met the book. It remains a staple of Swedish childhood reading and is often the first Lagerlöf work encountered outside Scandinavia, even though her adult fiction, such as *Gösta Berling's Saga*, is closer to the concerns of her other work.
masterNotes.form: The book is organized as a sequence of largely self-contained episodes strung along the geese's migration route, a structure inherited from its origin as a geography primer, so that each chapter can stand fairly independently while still advancing Nils's ongoing transformation. Lagerlöf writes in a plain, oral, fable-like register suited to a young audience, but folds in real Swedish place names, industries, and natural history rather than treating the landscape as generic fantasy backdrop. The shift in scale, a boy reduced to the size of a thumb and given a bird's-eye view of his own country, lets the narration treat familiar geography as newly strange, which is the book's central formal trick.
keyImages: Luther's Commentary and the New Testament laid open on the table, plus the good armchair dragged out for the purpose — the parents' elaborate staging to guarantee the sermon gets read.
The chest-lid's shadow, first noticed only as a dark shape in the windowsill mirror, before the boy understands what is causing it.
The elf's absorbed reverence for the embroidered cloth pulled from the chest, handled with more care than the boy is shown giving to anything.
whatToNotice: Notice that the parents' harsh assessment of the boy — lazy, cruel to animals — arrives through the mother's own thought, not the narrator's judgment.
Notice the elf is introduced only as a "dark shadow" in a mirror, well before the boy makes out any shape at all.
Notice how precisely the elf's clothing is catalogued — frock coat, buckled shoes, garters — for a creature no bigger than a hand's breadth.
Notice how much more sensory detail the mother's chest and its contents receive than almost anything else on the page.
Notice that the boy feels "not particularly frightened" of the elf specifically because of its size, in the sentence right before he starts plotting against it.
Notice that the sermon itself is never actually described — only the boy's drowsiness reading it, and the moment he startles awake.
discussionQuestions: Why might the book open with the parents' anxious verdict on the boy's character rather than with the elf itself?
What does the loving inventory of the mother's chest suggest about what this story values, before any magic has happened?
The boy feels no fear of the elf purely because of its size. What does that reveal about how he sees the world around him?

Beyond this excerpt: the elf has just been caught absorbed in something he clearly reveres, by a boy already weighing a prank. Without reading ahead, what do you expect a creature this meticulous to do once he realizes he's being watched?
furtherReading: Lagerlöf's *Gösta Berling's Saga* — her earlier, more adult novel, closer to the folkloric romanticism that made her reputation in Sweden.
Rudyard Kipling's *The Jungle Book* — a near-contemporary use of animal society to instruct and entertain a young reader.
Lagerlöf's 1909 Nobel Prize lecture materials — useful context for how her contemporaries situated this book within her larger body of work.

title: The End and the Beginning
author: Wisława Szymborska (translated by Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh)

masterNotes.context: Szymborska published "Koniec i początek" in Polish in 1993, in the collection of the same name, four years after the fall of Communist rule in Poland and not long after the wars in the former Yugoslavia had returned large-scale European war to daily headlines. Szymborska had lived through the German occupation of Poland and the destruction of Warsaw in the Second World War, and this poem's flat, almost administrative tone toward the labor of cleanup after war reads as hard-won rather than detached. The widely used English version is by Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh, whose translations did much to build Szymborska's English-language readership; it appears in *View with a Grain of Sand* (1995). Szymborska won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1996, three years after this poem's original publication, and it remains one of her most frequently cited works on the aftermath of war.
masterNotes.form: The poem proceeds as a plain, unornamented list of the unglamorous physical and social tasks that follow a war, refusing the elevated register readers might expect from a poem on this subject. Its short, declarative lines and matter-of-fact tone are characteristic of Szymborska's broader style, which favors irony and understatement over overt emotion, and the translators have preserved that flatness in English rather than smoothing it into more conventionally poetic language. The poem moves in stages, from immediate physical cleanup toward the slower work of memory and forgetting, ending on figures who were not present for the events at all — a structural choice that carries the poem's real argument about how history gets absorbed.
keyImages: The recurring image of physical rubble and debris being cleared by unnamed, uncelebrated workers, the poem's insistence on the unglamorous labor that always follows a war.
The figure who leans on a broom and still remembers how it was, a single human presence who has not yet caught up to the poem's larger movement toward forgetting.
The closing figures too young to have witnessed the events at all, lying in the grass and looking up at clouds, marking how completely the past can be absorbed by those who come after.
whatToNotice: Notice how deliberately the poem avoids naming any specific war, army, or nation, keeping its subject general rather than tied to one conflict.
Notice the shift partway through from concrete physical labor toward more abstract processes of memory and explanation.
Notice how the poem's tone stays level and almost bureaucratic throughout, even as its subject grows larger and more painful.
Notice who the poem chooses to end on, and how much distance separates that final figure from the poem's opening images.
discussionQuestions: Why might Szymborska have chosen a flat, list-like structure to describe the aftermath of war rather than a more overtly emotional one?
What is the effect of ending the poem with people who have no memory of the events it describes?
Does the poem's refusal to name a specific war make its argument more universal, or does it risk flattening real historical differences?
How does translation — the choice to keep the English plain rather than more lyrical — affect how this poem's argument lands for an English-language reader?
furtherReading: Wisława Szymborska, "Could Have" — another poem taking a similarly flat, ironic approach to catastrophe and survival.
Czesław Miłosz, *The Captive Mind* — a prose companion from another Polish writer on living through and after totalitarian upheaval.
Clare Cavanagh, *Lyric Poetry and Modern Politics* — discusses Szymborska's translated reception and the politics of postwar Polish poetry.

masterNotes.context: Morrison published *Beloved* in 1987, the first novel in what she later described as a loose trilogy continued by *Jazz* and *Paradise*. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1988, and Morrison went on to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, the first Black woman to do so. The novel's starting point, publicly acknowledged by Morrison, is the historical case of Margaret Garner, an enslaved woman who in 1856 killed her own daughter rather than see her returned to slavery after a failed escape from Kentucky into Ohio; Morrison used this as a point of departure rather than a case to reconstruct, inventing the novel's characters, setting, and events freely from there. The book is set mostly in and around Cincinnati in the years following the Civil War, among formerly enslaved people for whom the war's end did not end the past's claims on the present.
masterNotes.form: Morrison structures the novel non-chronologically, circling around a central act of violence that the narration approaches and retreats from repeatedly rather than disclosing in a single scene, so that the reader's understanding accumulates the way traumatic memory itself is shown to work for the characters. Point of view shifts among several characters, including extended passages of interior monologue that break from conventional syntax and punctuation, most notably in sections voicing Beloved herself. Present action and remembered past are given comparable narrative weight and are often not clearly demarcated, collapsing the distance a reader might expect between what is happening and what is being remembered.
keyImages: The house at 124 Bluestone Road, introduced as an active, almost sentient presence rather than a passive setting, its numbering used instead of a name throughout.
Sethe's back, scarred in a pattern another character reads as a tree, an image of the body carrying legible, permanent testimony to what has been done to it.
The color white, and its recurring, unsettling appearances, tracked by Baby Suggs as a private, wordless system of meaning.
The clearing in the woods where Baby Suggs preaches self-love to the formerly enslaved community, an image of collective healing set against the novel's private, individual wounds.
whatToNotice: Notice how long the novel withholds a full, direct account of the central act at its heart, and how it uses that delay rather than treating it as a twist.
Notice the shifts into fragmented, unpunctuated interior monologue and consider what kind of consciousness they seem to be rendering.
Pay attention to how physical scars and marks on the body are treated throughout as a kind of language the other characters have to learn to read.
Notice how present-tense domestic detail, cooking, chores, arrivals, is interrupted by memory without typographic warning, and track how you can tell the difference.
Notice the different relationships Sethe, Denver, and Paul D each have to the past, and how the novel keeps them distinct rather than treating trauma as a single shared experience.
discussionQuestions: What is gained by Morrison's choice to withhold and circle around the novel's central act rather than presenting it early and directly?
How does the novel's treatment of the body, scars, touch, appetite, shape its argument about what slavery did and did not take from its characters?
What role does the community around 124 Bluestone Road play in both isolating and eventually reaching Sethe?
How do Denver's and Paul D's differing relationships to Sethe's past change how you read her?
What does the novel's ending suggest about whether the past it depicts can, in any sense, be put down?
furtherReading: Toni Morrison's *Jazz* — the loosely connected novel that continues the informal trilogy *Beloved* begins.
Toni Morrison's essay collection *Playing in the Dark* — her own critical writing on race and the American literary imagination, useful context for her fiction's concerns.
William Faulkner's *Absalom, Absalom!* — an earlier American novel Morrison studied closely, built on a similarly circling, retrospective narrative method.
